lessons.title: Heapsort guarantees and memory locality
lessons.summary: Iterative heapsort gives constant extra space and a worst-case guarantee.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

### Properties

- **In-place**, O(1) extra memory (the iterative sift-down above needs no stack).
- **Worst case O(n log n)**, with no bad inputs to defend against.
- **Not stable.** The root swap sends elements across the array, past their equals.
- **Not adaptive.** A sorted input still costs linear times logarithmic growth (in fact, a sorted ascending array is not a max-heap, so it gets rearranged fully).

### Why it loses to quicksort in practice

On paper heapsort looks strictly better than quicksort. Heapsort can be slower on large arrays, but the ratio depends on implementation, data and hardware. Memory access and comparison counts help explain why:

- Sift-down jumps from index `i` to `2i + 1`. Near the root, frequently reused nodes may remain cached. Deeper in the heap, larger index gaps and less reuse can hurt locality; a different cache line does not by itself imply a cache miss.
- Quicksort's partition scans memory sequentially, which caches and prefetchers love.
- Heapsort also does more comparisons:

```formula
C_heap ≈ 2n log_2(n)
C_quick ≈ 1.39n log_2(n)
where
C_heap: a leading-term scale for the shown ordinary sift-down heapsort on demanding distinct-key inputs; each descent can compare both children, but early stops and duplicates can reduce the count
C_quick: the leading expected comparisons of randomized quicksort with independent uniform pivots on distinct keys
n: the number of elements
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n; about 20 for a million
≈: approximately equal to (leading term only)
In words: heapsort makes roughly 45% more comparisons than randomised quicksort (2 / 1.39 ≈ 1.44), around 40 million versus 28 million for a million elements.
```


So heapsort is used where its guarantees matter more than its speed:

- As the **fallback inside introsort** (C++ `std::sort`, .NET), triggered only when quicksort's recursion goes too deep.
- In the **Linux kernel**, whose `sort()` in `lib/sort.c` is a heapsort: no recursion, no allocation and no worst-case input to exploit.
- In embedded and real-time systems where a fixed upper bound on time and memory matters most.

## Key takeaways
- Iterative heapsort gives constant extra space and a worst-case guarantee.
- Comparison counts and nonsequential access affect speed, so benchmark claims require a workload and hardware.

## Further reading
- [Priority queues and heapsort — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/24pq/)

lessons.title: The comparison-sorting decision tree
lessons.summary: Each distinct-key ordering needs a distinguishable decision-tree leaf.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## The lower bound for comparison sorts

Merge sort, heapsort and good quicksorts are all linear times logarithmic growth. Is that a coincidence of the algorithms we happened to find, or a law?

It is a law, for **comparison sorts**: algorithms that learn about the input only by asking "is `a[i] < a[j]`?". That includes every sort so far.

### The decision tree

Model any comparison sort on inputs of size n as a binary tree:

- Each internal node is a comparison, such as `a[1] < a[2]?`.
- Each branch is an answer (yes or no).
- Each leaf is a final answer: the permutation that sorts the input.

Running the algorithm on a particular input traces one path from root to leaf. The number of comparisons is the length of that path.

Here is a decision tree for sorting three elements `a, b, c`:

```
              a<b?
          yes/    \no
         b<c?      a<c?
       y/   \n    y/   \n
    a,b,c  a<c?  b,a,c  b<c?
          y/  \n       y/  \n
       a,c,b c,a,b  b,c,a  c,b,a
```

Six leaves, one per ordering. The worst-case path has 3 comparisons.

### The counting argument

1. There are **n!** (n factorial: n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1) possible orderings of n distinct elements. The algorithm must be able to output each one, so the tree needs **at least n! leaves**. (If two orderings led to the same leaf, the algorithm would rearrange them identically and get one of them wrong.)
2. A binary tree of height h (its longest root-to-leaf path) has **at most 2ʰ leaves**, because the number of nodes can at most double at each level.
3. Put the two together:

```formula
2^h ≥ L ≥ n!
h ≥ log_2(n!)
log_2(3!) = log_2(6) ≈ 2.58
h ≥ ⌈2.58⌉ = 3
where
h: the height of the decision tree, which is the worst-case number of comparisons; a whole number
L: the number of leaves in the tree
n!: n factorial, n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1: the number of possible orderings of n distinct elements (3! = 6)
2^h: h copies of 2 multiplied together, the most leaves a binary tree of height h can have
log_2: the base-2 logarithm, which undoes "2 to the power": log_2(8) = 3
n: the number of elements being sorted; 3 in the example lines
⌈ ⌉: the ceiling: round up to the next whole number
≥: greater than or equal to
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a tree tall enough to hold one leaf per possible ordering must have height at least log_2(n!), so some input needs that many comparisons.
```

For three elements that is 3 comparisons, exactly what the tree above uses. The height is the worst-case number of comparisons, so this is the bound. Now estimate log₂(n!). For even input sizes, the largest half of the factorial’s factors are each at least half the input size. Odd sizes change only the rounding, preserving the asymptotic bound:

```formula
n! ≥ (n / 2)^{n/2}
log_2(n!) ≥ (n / 2) log_2(n / 2)
log_2(n!) = Ω(n log(n))
where
n!: n factorial, the product n × (n − 1) × … × 1
n: the positive integer input size; assume even n of at least two for the displayed half-factor derivation
(n / 2)^{n/2}: n/2 copies of n/2 multiplied together
log_2: the base-2 logarithm
log: the logarithm (the base does not matter inside Ω)
Ω: Big Omega: grows at least this fast, up to a constant factor
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: throwing away the smaller half of the factors and shrinking the rest to n/2 still leaves something that grows like n log n.
```

## Key takeaways
- Distinct permutations require separate leaves and a worst-case logarithmic-height decision tree.

## Further reading
- [Priority queues and heapsort — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/24pq/)
- [Merge sort and its complexity — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/22mergesort/)

questions.prompt: What is the minimum number of comparisons that **any** comparison sort needs, in the worst case, to sort 4 distinct elements?

options.explanation: 2⁴ = 16 leaves is fewer than the 4! = 24 orderings, so a decision tree of height 4 can't distinguish them all.
Correct. There are 24 orderings, and a binary tree needs height ⌈log₂ 24⌉ = 5 to have at least 24 leaves (2⁵ = 32).
6 comparisons suffice, but so do 5 (merge sort achieves 5 for 4 input items). The question asks for the minimum.
3 comparisons give at most 8 outcomes, far fewer than 24 possible orderings.

questions.workedExample:
1. Possible orderings of 4 distinct elements: 4! = 24.
2. Each comparison has 2 outcomes, so h comparisons distinguish at most 2ʰ cases.
3. Need enough leaves for every ordering:

```formula
2^h ≥ n! = 4! = 24
2^4 = 16 < 24
2^5 = 32 ≥ 24
h ≥ ⌈log_2(24)⌉ = ⌈4.58⌉ = 5
where
h: the height of the decision tree: the worst-case number of comparisons
n!: n factorial, n × (n − 1) × … × 1, the number of orderings; 4! = 24
n: the number of elements; here 4
2^h: h copies of 2 multiplied together, the most outcomes h yes/no comparisons can tell apart
log_2: the base-2 logarithm
⌈ ⌉: the ceiling: round up to a whole number
≥: greater than or equal to
<: less than
In words: 4 comparisons give only 16 outcomes for 24 orderings, so at least 5 are needed.
```

So at least 5 comparisons. Merge sort meets this bound for 4 elements: two merges of pairs (1 each) plus a final merge of 2 + 2 (at most 3) = 5.

questions.prompt: Using the decision-tree argument, what is the minimum worst-case number of comparisons to **merge** two sorted lists of 3 distinct elements each (all 6 elements distinct)?

options.explanation: Three comparisons distinguish only 8 outcomes, but there are 20 possible interleavings.
Four Boolean comparisons distinguish at most 16 outcomes, fewer than the 20 possible interleavings.
That is the base-two logarithm of 720 rounded up to ten, the bound for sorting 6 arbitrary elements. Merging has far fewer possible outcomes, since each list is already sorted.
Correct. There are 20 interleavings, requiring five comparisons in the worst case. The standard merge achieves this: at most 3 + 3 − 1 = 5 comparisons.

questions.workedExample:
1. Count the possible outputs. The merged list is fixed once you choose which 3 of the 6 positions hold the left list's elements:

```formula
C(6, 3) = 6! / (3! × 3!)
C(6, 3) = 720 / (6 × 6) = 20
2^4 = 16 < 20
2^5 = 32 ≥ 20
h ≥ 5
where
C(6, 3): "6 choose 3": the number of ways to pick 3 positions out of 6
6!: 6 factorial, 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 720 (3! = 6)
h: the height of the decision tree, the worst-case comparisons
2^4: 4 copies of 2 multiplied together (likewise 2^5)
≥: greater than or equal to
<: less than
In words: there are 20 possible merged orders, and only a tree of height 5 or more has room for 20 leaves.
```

2. A decision tree with height h has at most 2ʰ leaves, so h must be at least 5.

3. The standard merge uses at most 3 + 3 − 1 = 5 comparisons, so it is optimal for this case.

The same reasoning applies to any problem: the lower bound is the base-two logarithm of the number of possible answers.

lessons.title: Stirling estimates and average comparisons
lessons.summary: Stirling’s formula estimates factorial growth and the comparison lower bound.
lessons.body:
Here n is the number of input elements. This unit builds on the preceding decision-tree or recurrence proof.

**Stirling's approximation**, a standard estimate of n!, is sharper:

```formula
log_2(n!) ≈ n log_2(n) − 1.44n
log_2(10^6 !) ≈ 1.993 × 10^7 − 1.44 × 10^6
log_2(10^6 !) ≈ 1.85 × 10^7
where
log_2(n!): the base-2 logarithm of n factorial: an information lower bound on worst-case comparisons to sort n distinct elements; round upward for an integer comparison count
n: the number of elements; here a million (10^6)
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n; log_2(10^6) ≈ 19.93
1.44: log_2(e), where e ≈ 2.718 is the base of natural logarithms; it comes from Stirling's formula
10^6: ten to the power 6, a million; 10^7 is ten million
≈: approximately equal to (lower-order terms dropped)
In words: the information lower bound is n log_2 n minus about 1.44 comparisons per element: about 18.5 million for a million elements.
```

So **every comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case**. Merge sort and heapsort are **asymptotically optimal**: no comparison sort beats them by more than a constant factor.

The same argument works for the **average** case. A binary tree with many leaves cannot have all of them shallow:

```formula
d_avg ≥ log_2(N)
N = n!  ⇒  d_avg ≥ log_2(n!)
where
d_avg: the average depth of a leaf, with every leaf weighted equally: the average number of comparisons
N: reachable leaves of the Boolean comparison tree after pruning impossible branches, one for each distinct-key permutation
n!: n factorial, the number of orderings of n distinct elements
n: the number of elements
log_2: the base-2 logarithm
⇒: "which means"
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: a binary tree with N leaves has average leaf depth at least log_2(N), so averaged over all n! orderings a comparison sort still needs about log_2(n!) comparisons.
```

Averaging over all distinct-key permutations gives Ω(n log n), including expected comparisons of correct randomized sorts. This is not a bound for every nonuniform input distribution.

## Key takeaways
- Stirling’s formula estimates factorial growth and the comparison lower bound.
- The uniform-permutation average also requires logarithmic decision-tree depth.

## Further reading
- [Priority queues and heapsort — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/24pq/)
- [Merge sort and its complexity — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/22mergesort/)

lessons.title: Tight bounds and what they exclude
lessons.summary: Merge sort’s comparison count is close to the information lower bound.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

### Real numbers

The last column rounds the base-two logarithm of the number of permutations upward. For four elements, 24 possible permutations require five comparisons in the worst case.

```formula
h ≥ ⌈log_2(n!)⌉
h ≥ ⌈log_2(24)⌉ = 5
where
h: worst-case number of Boolean key comparisons
n: number of distinct elements; four here
!: factorial, product of the integers from one through n
log_2: base-two logarithm
⌈ ⌉: ceiling, round upward
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: A binary comparison tree must be deep enough to distinguish all 24 permutations.
```

| n | n! | min worst-case compares |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 6 | 3 |
| 4 | 24 | 5 |
| 5 | 120 | 7 |
| 1,000,000 | huge | ≈ 18.5 million |

How close does merge sort get? Use the exact worst-case count for top-down merge sort from the relevant unit in this module:

```formula
C_w = n⌈log_2(n)⌉ − 2^{⌈log_2(n)⌉} + 1
C_w = 10^6 × 20 − 2^20 + 1
C_w = 18951425 ≈ 1.895 × 10^7
r = C_w / log_2(n!)
r ≈ 1.895 × 10^7 / (1.849 × 10^7) ≈ 1.025
where
C_w: the most comparisons top-down merge sort makes on any input of n elements
n: the number of elements, a million (10^6)
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n, about 19.93 here
⌈ ⌉: the ceiling: round up to a whole number, so ⌈19.93⌉ = 20
2^20: 20 copies of 2 multiplied together, 1,048,576
log_2(n!): the information lower bound on worst-case comparisons, about 18.49 million here; an exact optimum may be higher
r: the ratio of merge sort's worst case to that minimum
10^6: ten to the power 6, a million; 10^7 is ten million
≈: approximately equal to
In words: in its worst case, merge sort uses only about 2.5% more comparisons than the theoretical minimum for a million elements.
```

So merge sort's worst case is within about 3% of the absolute minimum (the rough estimate input size times its base-two logarithm would put it within about 8%). There is little left to win on comparison counts; real-world gains come from cache behaviour, branch prediction and exploiting existing order.

> [!note] Exact optimal sorting is hard
> For five items the bound says 7 comparisons. Plain merge sort needs 8 in the worst case. The Ford–Johnson "merge insertion" algorithm achieves 7, but finding the true minimum for every n is an open problem.

### What the bound does not say

- **It only covers comparisons.** If you can look inside the keys (use an integer as an array index, or inspect digits), the decision-tree model does not apply. That is how counting sort and radix sort run in linear time (covered later in this module).
- **It is about the worst or average case.** An adaptive sort can be O(n) on already sorted input. The bound applies to the set of all n! inputs; a more refined version says you need about log₂(number of possible inputs) comparisons, which is why sorting data with few runs or few distinct values can be faster.
- **It has consequences elsewhere.** Anything that would let you sort is also Ω(n log n). For example, building a binary search tree from n items and reading it in order sorts them, so building a comparison-based BST from arbitrary distinct unsorted keys has Ω(n log n) worst-case cost. Locating one of one more insertion position than the existing item count with Boolean order tests requires a matching minimum number of tests in the worst case (formula below), achieved by lower-bound binary search.

```formula
q ≥ ⌈log_2(n + 1)⌉
q ≥ ⌈log_2(1024)⌉ = 10
where
q: the worst-case number of yes/no order tests needed to find where a new key belongs
n: the number of elements already in the sorted array; here 1,023, which leaves 1,024 possible insertion positions
log_2: the base-2 logarithm
⌈ ⌉: the ceiling: round up to the next whole number
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: each yes/no test can at best halve the possible positions, so choosing among n + 1 positions needs about log_2(n + 1) tests.
```

## Key takeaways
- Merge sort’s comparison count is close to the information lower bound.
- The bound covers comparison-based worst or uniform-average cases, rather than sorted inputs or digit-indexing methods.

## Further reading
- [Priority queues and heapsort — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/24pq/)
- [Merge sort and its complexity — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/22mergesort/)

questions.prompt:
The Ω(n log n) worst-case lower bound applies to which of these algorithms? Select all that apply.

Here n is the number of input elements; other symbols are defined in this question’s formula cards; d is the number of digit passes. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Merge sort
options.explanation: Correct. It only compares elements, so it obeys the bound, and it meets it: Θ(n log n).

options.text: Insertion sort
options.explanation: Correct. It is a comparison sort. Its worst case, Θ(n²), is above the bound, which is consistent; the bound is a floor, not a ceiling.

options.text: Counting sort
options.explanation: No. Counting sort uses keys as array indices rather than comparing them, so the decision-tree model doesn't describe it.

options.text: Heapsort
options.explanation: Correct. It is a comparison sort and matches the bound with Θ(n log n).

options.text: LSD radix sort
options.explanation: No. Radix sort inspects digits and uses them as indices; it never asks 'is a < b?', so the bound doesn't apply.

questions.workedExample:
The bound covers algorithms whose **only** way to learn about the order is comparing pairs.

| Algorithm | Comparison sort? | Worst case |
|---|---|---|
| Merge sort | Yes | O(n log n) |
| Insertion sort | Yes | Quadratic |
| Heapsort | Yes | O(n log n) |
| Counting sort | No | Input size plus key-range size |
| Radix sort | No | Digit passes times input-plus-base |

Here n is the number of elements, k the number of possible key values, d the number of digits and b the base (values per digit).

The bound says a comparison sort has a logarithmic-factor linear lower bound. Insertion sort is slower, which the bound allows.

questions.prompt: A vendor claims their new comparison-based sort handles **any** input of 1,000,000 distinct keys with at most 15 million comparisons. What should you conclude?

options.text: It's plausible: 15 million exceeds the one million input size
options.explanation: Being above n isn't enough. The lower bound is the base-2 logarithm of n! (the number of orderings of n keys), which is far bigger than n.

options.text: It's plausible if they use a clever pivot
options.explanation: No pivot strategy beats the information-theoretic bound; it applies to every comparison sort.

options.text: It's impossible: any comparison sort needs at least about 18.5 million comparisons in the worst case
options.explanation: Correct. There are 10⁶! orderings and 15 million comparisons can distinguish at most the number of leaves in a height-15-million binary tree, which is fewer. The claim must be wrong (or the sort isn't purely comparison-based, or it only works on special inputs).

options.text: It's impossible because any sort needs quadratic comparisons
options.explanation: Quadratic cost in the input size applies to simple sorts like insertion sort, not to all sorts. Merge sort needs only about 20 million here.

questions.workedExample:
1. Number of possible orderings: n! (n factorial) for one million keys.
2. Use Stirling's approximation:

```formula
log_2(n!) ≈ n log_2(n) − 1.44n
n log_2(n) ≈ 10^6 × 19.93
n log_2(n) ≈ 1.993 × 10^7
1.44n = 1.44 × 10^6
log_2(n!) ≈ 1.85 × 10^7
where
n: the number of distinct keys; here 10^6, a million
n!: n factorial, n × (n − 1) × … × 1: the number of orderings
log_2: the base-2 logarithm
1.44: log_2(e), where e ≈ 2.718 is the base of natural logarithms
10^6: ten to the power 6; 10^7 is ten million
≈: approximately equal to
In words: sorting a million keys needs at least about 18.5 million comparisons in the worst case.
```

3. A height-15-million binary tree has fewer leaves than the number of distinct-key permutations. It cannot distinguish every ordering.

The claim is impossible for a general comparison sort. Perhaps they measured on nearly sorted inputs, or they're using radix-style tricks.

questions.prompt:
A colleague says they've designed a comparison-based priority queue with O(1) `insert` and O(1) `extract_min`, both worst case. Why must this be wrong?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Priority queues can't be implemented in arrays
options.explanation: They can: a binary heap is an array. The issue is with the time bounds.

options.text: Because you could then sort n items in O(n) time with comparisons alone, violating the Ω(n log n) lower bound
options.explanation: Correct. Insert all n items (O(n)) then extract the minimum n times (O(n)) and you have a comparison sort in O(n), which is impossible.

options.text: Because extract_min must always scan every element
options.explanation: Not necessarily: a heap finds the minimum in O(1) and removes it in O(log n). It's the combination of both operations being O(1) that's impossible.

options.text: Because O(1) insert is impossible for any data structure
options.explanation: An unsorted list has O(1) insert. Fibonacci heaps even have O(1) amortised insert; their extract_min is O(log n) amortised.

questions.workedExample:
This is a **reduction** to sorting:

```
for x in items:   pq.insert(x)
out = [pq.extract_min()
       for _ in items]
```

1. With O(1) operations (constant time each), this costs:

```formula
T = n O(1) + n O(1) = O(n)
where
T: the total time of the sort built from the priority queue
n: the number of items
O(1): at most a constant amount of time per operation
O(n): time growing at most in proportion to n
In words: n constant-time inserts plus n constant-time extractions is linear time.
```
2. It outputs the items in sorted order using only comparisons.
3. But every comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons. Contradiction.

So at least one of the operations must cost Ω(log n) (amortised). Binary heaps pay O(log n) for both; Fibonacci heaps make insert O(1) amortised but extract_min stays O(log n).

questions.prompt:
Which statements about the comparison-sort lower bound are true? Select all that apply.

Here n is the number of input elements; other symbols are defined in this question’s formula cards. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: It also applies to the average case, not just the worst case
options.explanation: Correct. In any binary tree the average leaf depth is at least the base-2 logarithm of the number of leaves, so the average over all n! orderings of n inputs is also Ω(n log n).

options.text: Radix sort running in linear time shows the proof is flawed
options.explanation: No. Radix sort isn't a comparison sort, so the decision-tree model never applied to it. The proof is sound for its stated model.

options.text: An adaptive sort that runs in O(n) on already sorted input doesn't contradict it
options.explanation: Correct. The bound is over all n! inputs; individual easy inputs can be handled in O(n). Timsort does exactly this.

options.text: Stirling’s estimate is a leading logarithmic term minus about 1.44 per input item
options.explanation: Correct. By Stirling's approximation (worked example), the conversion coefficient is about 1.443, as defined in the formula card.

options.text: It applies to any algorithm, including those that hash keys or use them as array indices
options.explanation: No. Those operations extract more than one bit of information per step, which is exactly how counting and radix sort escape the bound.

questions.workedExample:
The proof models an algorithm as a binary decision tree in which each node is a comparison.

- **Average case:** the number of leaves covers every permutation, and average leaf depth is bounded by the base-two logarithm of that count. True.
- **Radix/counting:** they index arrays with key values, a k-way branch, not 2-way. Outside the model. The second and fifth claims are false.
- **Adaptive sorts:** the bound is about the hardest inputs. Sorted input is one easy leaf at depth one fewer than the input size. True.
- **Stirling:** true, as follows.

```formula
ln(n!) ≈ n ln(n) − n
log_2(n!) ≈ n log_2(n) − n log_2(e)
log_2(n!) ≈ n log_2(n) − 1.44n
where
n: the number of elements
n!: n factorial, the number of orderings
ln: the natural logarithm, base e
e: Euler's number, about 2.718
log_2: the base-2 logarithm; log_2(e) ≈ 1.443
≈: approximately equal to (an O(log n) term is dropped)
In words: dividing Stirling's natural-log formula by ln 2 turns it into base 2, giving n log_2 n minus about 1.44 per element.
```

lessons.title: Counting sort and stable output slots
lessons.summary: Prefix counts locate each key’s output block.
lessons.body:
The last lesson proved that any sort which only *compares* elements needs Ω(n log n) comparisons, where n is the number of elements and Ω (Big Omega) means "at least this growth rate, up to a constant factor". The way around that is to stop comparing. If keys are small integers, or can be broken into small integer digits, you can use them directly as **array indices**. An index lookup answers "which of k buckets does this go in?" in one step, which is far more information than a yes/no comparison.

That is the whole trick behind counting sort, radix sort and bucket sort. The catch is that they only work when the keys have the right shape.

## Counting sort

**Assumption:** keys are integers in a known range `0..k−1`: k is the number of possible key values, and n is the number of elements.

Count how many times each key occurs, then use running totals to work out where each key's block starts in the output.

```python
def counting_sort(a, key, k):
    count = [0] * k
    for x in a:
        # Count the frequency of each
        # integer key.
        count[key(x)] += 1
    # prefix sums: end of each key's slot
    for v in range(1, k):
        # Convert frequencies into block
        # endpoints.
        count[v] += count[v - 1]
    out = [None] * len(a)
    for x in reversed(a):  # keeps it stable
        # Fill each block from its last free
        # slot.
        count[key(x)] -= 1
        # Reverse input traversal preserves
        # ties.
        out[count[key(x)]] = x
    return out
```

Trace on `[2, 5, 3, 0, 2, 3, 0, 3]` with k = 6:

```
value:   0  1  2  3  4  5
count:   2  0  2  3  0  1
prefix:  2  2  4  7  7  8
```

The prefix sum says "values ≤ 3 occupy the first 7 slots", so the last 3 goes in slot 6, the next 3 in slot 5, and so on. Output: `[0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 5]`.

- **Time:** O(n + k): one pass to count, one over the k counters, one to place.
- **Space:** O(n + k) for the output and counts.
- **Stable**, because the final pass walks the input **backwards** and fills each block from its end. Walk forwards while decrementing and equal keys come out reversed. Stability is not a nicety here: radix sort depends on it.

If you are sorting bare integers (no attached data), you can skip the output array and just write each value `count[v]` times. The prefix-sum version is needed when the key is attached to a record.

### When counting sort works and when it does not

- Exam scores 0 to 100 for 2 million students: k = 101, n = 2,000,000. Linear and very fast.
- Ages, HTTP status codes, bytes (k = 256), days of the year: all good fits.
- 1,000 arbitrary 32-bit integers: about 4.3 billion possible values, so about 4.3 billion counters, whatever n is. The counts alone need 16 GiB (formula below); Python lists have different, larger overhead. Hopeless.

```formula
k = 2^32 ≈ 4.3 × 10^9
M = k × 4 B = 2^34 B
M = 16 GiB ≈ 17.2 GB
where
k: the number of possible key values: a 32-bit integer can take 2^32 values
M: the memory the counter array needs
2^32: 32 copies of 2 multiplied together, 4,294,967,296
B: bytes; each counter here is a 4-byte integer
GiB: gibibyte, 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 bytes
GB: gigabyte, 1,000,000,000 bytes
≈: approximately equal to
In words: one 4-byte counter for each of the 4.3 billion possible values needs 16 GiB, even to sort only 1,000 numbers.
```

The rule: counting sort is great when **k is O(n)** or smaller. When k is much larger than n, use radix sort.

## Key takeaways
- Prefix counts locate each key’s output block.
- Reverse placement preserves ties; the key range controls counter memory.

## Further reading
- [LSD and MSD radix sorting — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/51radix/)

questions.prompt:
You need to sort 2 million exam results by score, where every score is an integer from 0 to 100. What is counting sort's running time here?

Here n is the number of input elements; other symbols are defined in this question’s formula cards. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: O(n log n), like any sort
options.explanation: Counting sort isn't a comparison sort, so the logarithmic-factor linear lower bound for comparison sorts (n is the number of records) doesn't apply to it.

options.text: O(n²)
options.explanation: Counting sort never compares pairs of elements; it does a fixed number of passes.

options.text: O(n + k) with 101 possible key values, so effectively linear in n
options.explanation: Correct. One pass counts the 2 million scores, one pass over 101 counters builds prefix sums, and one pass places each record.

options.text: O(k) only, since there are only 101 possible scores
options.explanation: Every one of the n records still has to be read and placed, so the cost includes n.

questions.workedExample:
Counting sort makes one pass over the records to count, one over the counters, and one more over the records to place them:

```formula
T = n + k + n
T = 2000000 + 101 + 2000000 ≈ 4 × 10^6
C ≈ n log_2(n) ≈ 2 × 10^6 × 21
C ≈ 4.2 × 10^7
where
T: a simplified pass-length proxy for counting and placement; counter/output initialization and individual instructions add work
n: the number of records; here 2,000,000
k: the number of possible keys; scores 0 to 100 give 101
C: roughly the comparisons an n log n comparison sort would make
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n; log_2(2,000,000) ≈ 21
10^6: ten to the power 6, a million; 10^7 is ten million
≈: approximately equal to
In words: counting and placement visit four million records, plus the small counter pass. This pass-length proxy and a comparison count are different operations, so their ratio is not a measured speedup.
```

That is O(n + k). Because k is tiny relative to n, counting sort is ideal.

questions.prompt:
Which of these is the best fit for counting sort?

Here n is the number of input elements; other symbols are defined in this question’s formula cards. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: 50 million people sorted by age in whole years (0–130)
options.explanation: Correct. 131 possible keys is tiny compared with 50 million inputs, so O(n + k) is essentially linear and the counts fit in a few hundred bytes.

options.text: 1,000 arbitrary 64-bit integers
options.explanation: k = 2⁶⁴: the count array would be astronomically large. Radix sort or a comparison sort is the right tool.

options.text: 10,000 strings sorted with a locale-aware collation
options.explanation: Collation rules don't map strings to small integer keys; a comparison sort with a key function is the practical choice.

options.text: 100 floating-point measurements
options.explanation: Floats aren't small-range integers, and a standard library comparison sort is a sensible baseline for 100 items; fastest requires measurement.

questions.workedExample:
Counting sort is O(n + k) time and O(n + k) space, where n is the number of records and k the number of possible key values, so it shines when **k is not much larger than n**.

| Data | n | k | Fit? |
|---|---|---|---|
| ages | 5×10⁷ | 131 | great |
| 64-bit ints | 10³ | 1.8×10¹⁹ | no |
| collated strings | 10⁴ | n/a | no |
| 100 floats | 10² | n/a | no |

questions.prompt:
Stable counting sort (the lesson's version, final loop walking the input **backwards**) sorts these records by their number. At which output index does the record `(1,'u')` land?

```
[(1,'p'), (0,'q'), (3,'r'),
 (1,'s'), (3,'t'), (1,'u')]
```

options.explanation: Index 1 is where the *first* key-1 record, (1,'p'), goes. (1,'u') is the last key-1 record in the input, so it takes the last key-1 slot.
Correct. Prefix sums give count[1] = 4, so key-1 records occupy indices 1–3. (1,'u') is met first in the backward scan and takes index 3.
Index 5 is the last slot overall, which belongs to the largest key, 3.
Index 4 is the first slot for key 3. The key-1 block ends at index 3.

questions.workedExample:
1. Counts per key 0..3:

```
key:    0  1  2  3
count:  1  3  0  2
prefix: 1  4  4  6
```

2. Prefix 4 for key 1 means "keys ≤ 1 fill indices 0–3", so key 1 owns indices 1, 2, 3.
3. Walk the input backwards. The first record met is (1,'u'): decrement count[1] to 3 and place it at index 3.
4. Later (1,'s') goes to 2 and (1,'p') to 1.

Final: `[q, p, s, u, r, t]`. The key-1 records keep their input order p, s, u: stable.

questions.prompt: Someone uses counting sort on 1,000 arbitrary **32-bit** unsigned integers, allocating one 4-byte counter per possible value. Roughly how much memory does the count array need?

options.text: About 4 KB
options.explanation: That's one counter per *element*. Counting sort needs one counter per possible *value*: 2³² of them.

options.text: About 4 MB
options.explanation: That would be about a million counters, only enough for 20-bit values.

options.text: About 128 bytes
options.explanation: 32 bits × 4 bytes would be a per-bit table, but base-2 radix sorting needs just two counters per pass, not counting sort over the whole value.

options.text: 16 GiB, about 17 GB
options.explanation: Correct. About 4.3 billion four-byte counters need 16 GiB (approximately 17.2 billion bytes), even though 1,000 four-byte inputs occupy only 4 KB. The worked formula defines those units.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
k = 2^32 = 4294967296
M = k × 4 B = 17179869184 B
M = 16 GiB
where
k: the number of possible 32-bit values, one counter each
M: the memory the count array needs
2^32: 32 copies of 2 multiplied together
B: bytes; each counter is 4 bytes
GiB: gibibyte, 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 bytes
In words: 4.3 billion counters of 4 bytes each is 16 GiB, about 17.2 billion bytes.
```

And even if you had the memory, the prefix-sum pass alone touches 4.3 billion counters to sort 1,000 numbers. With millions of times more possible values than records, counting sort is hopeless.

The fix is radix sort: 4 passes with base 256 use a 256-entry table each, or simply a comparison sort, since 1,000 × log₂ 1,000 ≈ 10,000 comparisons is trivial.

questions.prompt:
A developer "simplifies" counting sort by walking the input **forwards** in the final placement loop, still decrementing `count[key]` before placing. They then use it as the digit pass in LSD radix sort. What happens?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Nothing: counting sort is stable either way
options.explanation: Forward iteration with decrementing fills each key's block from its end, so the first equal key lands last: the order of equals is reversed.

options.text: Each pass still groups by digit correctly, but equal digits come out reversed, so the radix sort produces wrongly ordered output
options.explanation: Correct. Each pass is now 'anti-stable'. Ties on the current digit reverse the order from earlier passes, so lower digits end up scrambled.

options.text: It crashes with an index error
options.explanation: The indices are the same set of slots, just filled in a different order; there's no out-of-range access.

options.text: It becomes O(n²)
options.explanation: The loop does the same amount of work in either direction; only the order of equal keys changes.

questions.workedExample:
Counting sort on `[(1,'a'), (0,'b'), (1,'c')]` with a forward placement loop:

```
prefix: count[0]=1, count[1]=3
(1,a): count[1]=2 -> out[2]
(0,b): count[0]=0 -> out[0]
(1,c): count[1]=1 -> out[1]
out = [b, c, a]   a,c reversed!
```

In LSD radix sort, take 21 and 25 sorted by ones as `[21, 25]`. The tens pass ties them and reverses them to `[25, 21]`. Wrong.

Either walk backwards while decrementing, or walk forwards using the *start* of each block (exclusive prefix sums) and increment.

lessons.title: Stable LSD radix passes
lessons.summary: Start with the least significant digit and preserve previous lower-digit order.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Radix sort

**Idea:** break each key into digits and sort one digit at a time with a stable counting sort.

**LSD (least significant digit) radix sort** starts with the last digit and works left. Sort `[170, 45, 75, 90, 802, 24, 2, 66]` in base 10:

```
ones:  [170, 90, 802, 2, 24, 45, 75, 66]
tens:  [802, 2, 24, 45, 66, 170, 75, 90]
100s:  [2, 24, 45, 66, 75, 90, 170, 802]
```

Look at the tens pass: 802 and 2 both have tens digit 0. The ones pass had already put 802 before 2, and because the sort is stable, they keep that order. Once a pass is done, ties on the current digit are broken by the lower digits, which were sorted earlier. **Without stability, LSD radix sort gives wrong answers.**

```python
def radix_sort(a, base=256):
    if type(base) is not int or base < 2:
        raise ValueError("base >= 2")
    if any(type(x) is not int or x < 0
           for x in a):
        raise ValueError("nonnegative ints")
    if not a:
        return a
    # Start at the least significant digit.
    exp = 1
    while max(a) // exp > 0:
        digit = lambda x: (x // exp) % base
        # Keep the order established by
        # prior digits.
        a = counting_sort(a, digit, base)
        # Move to the next more significant
        # digit.
        exp *= base
    return a
```

## Key takeaways
- Start with the least significant digit and preserve previous lower-digit order.
- Every digit pass must be stable for the final ordering to be correct.

## Further reading
- [LSD and MSD radix sorting — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/51radix/)

questions.prompt: Why must each digit pass in LSD radix sort use a **stable** sort?

options.text: Stable sorts are faster
options.explanation: Speed isn't the issue; an unstable pass gives *wrong* answers.

options.text: To save memory
options.explanation: Stability doesn't reduce memory: stable counting sort needs an output buffer.

options.text: It doesn't matter; any sort works for each pass
options.explanation: It matters. 21 and 25 tie on the tens digit; an unstable tens pass may output 25 before 21, undoing the ones-digit order, and no later pass looks at the ones digit again.

options.text: So that ties on the current digit keep the order established by the earlier, less significant digits
options.explanation: Correct. After sorting by tens, two numbers with the same tens digit must stay in ones-digit order. An unstable pass could scramble them.

questions.workedExample:
Consider 21 and 25 after the ones pass: `[21, 25]` (1 < 5).

Tens pass: both have tens digit 2, so they tie.

- **Stable:** keeps `[21, 25]`. Correct.
- **Unstable:** may output `[25, 21]`. Wrong, and no later pass will fix it, because later passes only look at higher digits.

LSD radix sort works only because each pass preserves the work of the previous ones on ties.

questions.prompt:
LSD radix sort in base 10 is applied to the list below. What does the list look like after the **first** pass?

```
[329, 457, 657, 839, 436, 720, 355]
```

options.explanation: That is the fully sorted result, after all three passes. One pass only orders by the ones digit.
LSD starts at the least significant digit (ones), not the hundreds. Starting with the most significant digit is MSD radix sort.
Correct. Ordered by ones digit: 0 (720), 5 (355), 6 (436), 7 (457, 657, in input order), 9 (329, 839, in input order).
This has the right digit groups but reverses ties. A stable pass must keep 457 before 657 and 329 before 839.

questions.workedExample:
Ones digits: 329→9, 457→7, 657→7, 839→9, 436→6, 720→0, 355→5.

Group stably by that digit:

```
0: 720
5: 355
6: 436
7: 457, 657   (input order)
9: 329, 839   (input order)
-> [720, 355, 436, 457, 657, 329, 839]
```

The tens pass then gives `[720, 329, 436, 839, 355, 457, 657]` and the hundreds pass the sorted list.

lessons.title: Radix width, base and pass costs
lessons.summary: Pass count depends on key width and digit base.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

### What radix sort really costs

Each pass is a counting sort over one digit, so it costs O(n + b) for a digit with b possible values. Multiply by the number of passes:

```formula
T = O(d(n + b))
P = dn = 4 × 10^7
C = n log_2(n) ≈ 10^7 × 23.3 ≈ 2.3 × 10^8
where
T: the running time of LSD radix sort
O: Big O: grows at most this fast, up to a constant factor
d: the number of digits per key, which is the number of passes; 4 here (32-bit keys, one byte per digit)
n: the number of keys; 10 million (10^7) here
b: the base: how many values one digit can take; 256 here, one byte
P: the total output placements across all the passes
C: roughly the comparisons an n log n comparison sort would make on the same keys
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n; log_2(10^7) ≈ 23.3
10^7: ten to the power 7, ten million
≈: approximately equal to
In words: radix sort does d passes, each touching every key once plus a table of b counters; for 32-bit keys in base 256 that is 4 passes.
```

For 32-bit unsigned integers with base 256 (one byte per digit): four passes cover the full key width. A 256-entry table of four-byte counters needs 1 KiB and fits in many L1 data caches; Python counter objects have different storage overhead. For 10 million keys, that is 40 million output placements across the digit passes, plus counting reads and other overhead, versus roughly 230 million comparisons for an linear times logarithmic growth sort.

> [!warning] Radix sort depends on key width
> The bound above assumes each digit operation costs a constant amount. It is "linear" only because the number of digits is treated as fixed. Python arbitrary-size integer division has its own bit cost.

How many digits are there? It depends on the key width, not on n, but n distinct keys need at least enough digits to tell them apart:

```formula
d = ⌈w / log_2(b)⌉
d = 32 / log_2(256) = 32 / 8 = 4
d ≥ ⌈log_b(n)⌉
where
d: the number of digits (passes)
w: the key width in bits; 32 here
b: the base, the number of values one digit can take; 256 here
log_2(b): the number of bits in one digit; log_2(256) = 8
log_b(n): the logarithm of n to base b: the power you raise b to in order to get n
n: the number of keys, all distinct
⌈ ⌉: the ceiling: round up to the next whole number
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: 32-bit keys in base 256 always take 4 passes, and n distinct keys can never fit in fewer than log_b(n) digits.
```

That lower bound on d does not imply an upper bound: keys can be much wider. Fixed 32- or 64-bit keys give a fixed number of passes, with at most 2³² or 2⁶⁴ distinct values.
Choosing the base is a trade-off. Base 2¹⁶ means 2 passes for 32-bit keys, but clearing 65,536 counters costs more and the table may exceed the target CPU cache. Base 2⁸ uses a smaller table. The best base depends on counter representation, hardware and workload.

## Key takeaways
- Pass count depends on key width and digit base.
- Large counter tables and arbitrary-precision digit operations change practical cost.

## Further reading
- [LSD and MSD radix sorting — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/51radix/)

questions.prompt: You radix sort 100 million unsigned **64-bit** keys using one byte per digit (base 256). How many counting-sort passes are needed?

options.explanation: Four byte-sized digits cover 32 bits, not 64.
Correct. 64 bits ÷ 8 bits per digit = 8 passes, each over all 100 million keys with a 256-entry count table.
That is base 2 (one bit per pass). Base 256 handles 8 bits per pass.
That is about log₂(10⁸), the depth of a comparison sort. Radix passes depend on key width, not n.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
d = w / log_2(b)
d = 64 / log_2(2^8) = 64 / 8 = 8
d = 64 / log_2(2^16) = 64 / 16 = 4
where
d: the number of counting-sort passes (digits per key)
w: the key width in bits; here 64
b: the base: how many values one digit can take; 2^8 = 256 or 2^16 = 65,536
log_2(b): the bits in one digit; log_2(2^8) = 8
2^8: 8 copies of 2 multiplied together (likewise 2^16)
In words: divide the key width by the bits per digit: 8 passes in base 256, 4 in base 65,536.
```

Base 2¹⁶ halves the passes but needs a 65,536-entry count table per pass, which may exceed the target L1 cache capacity. Base 256 (8 passes, 256-entry table) is the common choice.

The eight passes make 800 million output placements, plus counting reads and other overhead. A logarithmic-factor comparison model suggests about 2.7 billion comparisons on 100 million keys; these are different operations, so the counts do not establish a runtime ratio.

questions.prompt:
Which statements about the cost of radix sort are true? Select all that apply.

Here n is the number of input elements; d is the number of digit passes. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: LSD radix sort with d digits in base b costs O(d·(n + b))
options.explanation: Correct. Each of the d passes is a counting sort over n elements with b counters.

options.text: Distinct keys need enough digit combinations to represent every key, so key width is not free
options.explanation: Correct. Distinct keys need enough digits to tell n values apart. Radix sort wins because real keys have a fixed width and each step is a cheap index, not because logarithmic key width disappears.

options.text: A larger base is always faster, because it means fewer passes
options.explanation: No. Base 2¹⁶ halves the passes for 32-bit keys, but its 65,536-entry table costs more to clear and may exceed the target cache capacity; fewer passes do not guarantee less time.

options.text: LSD radix sort is in-place
options.explanation: No. Each stable counting pass writes into an O(n) output buffer.

options.text: MSD radix sort on strings can stop examining characters once a bucket holds a single string
options.explanation: Correct. It only looks at as many characters as needed to distinguish each string, which is why it suits variable-length keys.

questions.workedExample:
Put numbers on it for 10⁷ 32-bit keys:

| Base | Passes | Table |
|---|---|---|
| 2⁸ | 4 | 256 counters |
| 2¹⁶ | 2 | 65,536 counters |
| 2 | 32 | 2 |

Base 2 makes 32 passes: far too many. Base 2¹⁶ makes only 2 passes but with a large, cache-unfriendly table. Choose the base by measuring the actual representation, hardware and workload.

```formula
T = O(d(n + b))
d ≥ ⌈log_b(n)⌉
d ≥ ⌈log_b(10^7)⌉ = ⌈2.9⌉ = 3
where
T: the running time of LSD radix sort
O: Big O: grows at most this fast, up to a constant factor
d: the number of digits per key (passes)
n: the number of keys; 10 million (10^7) here
b: the base, values per digit; 256 in the last line (log_256(10^7) ≈ 2.9)
log_b(n): the logarithm of n to base b: the power you raise b to in order to get n
⌈ ⌉: the ceiling: round up to a whole number
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: d passes each cost about n + b, and n distinct keys need at least log_b(n) digits: 3 bytes for 10 million distinct keys.
```

That is a lower bound on width, not an upper bound: keys may be much wider (32-bit keys use 4 bytes), and fixed-width keys give a bounded number of passes.

lessons.title: Radix sorting strings and signed keys
lessons.summary: MSD sorting follows distinguishing prefixes and can stop early.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

### MSD radix sort and strings

**MSD (most significant digit)** radix sort starts from the first digit, splits into buckets, and recurses into each bucket. It suits variable-length strings: you can stop as soon as a bucket has one element, and you never look at characters beyond the distinguishing prefix. Stability depends on the MSD implementation; in-place variants may be unstable. Many implementations switch to insertion sort for small buckets. Sorting strings this way is the basis of suffix array construction and some fast string-sorting libraries.

### Negative numbers and floats

- **Signed integers:** flip the sign bit before sorting (XOR with `0x80000000` for 32-bit), so negatives come first.
- **IEEE-754 floats:** positive floats already sort correctly as unsigned integers. For negatives, flip all the bits; for positives, flip just the sign bit. For non-NaN IEEE binary values this maps numerical order to unsigned-key order. Specify NaN placement and whether -0.0 and +0.0 must be treated as equivalent; simple bit transforms alone do not establish that policy.

## Key takeaways
- MSD sorting follows distinguishing prefixes and can stop early.
- Signed and floating keys require an order-preserving encoding and an explicit NaN policy.

## Further reading
- [LSD and MSD radix sorting — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/51radix/)
- [NVIDIA radix transforms and floating-point policies](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cccl/blob/main/cub/cub/device/device_radix_sort.cuh)

questions.prompt: A radix sort reads the raw bits of signed 32-bit two’s-complement integers as unsigned keys. Which preprocessing step makes the integer order run from the most negative value through zero to the most positive?

options.text: Flip the sign bit of every key
options.explanation: Correct: the negative half moves below the nonnegative half while ordering inside each half is retained.

options.text: Leave every bit unchanged
options.explanation: Raw unsigned order places nonnegative encodings before negative encodings, so the halves appear in the wrong order.

options.text: Flip every bit of every key
options.explanation: That reverses bitwise unsigned order within each half; the integer transform only needs the sign bit flipped.

options.text: Use an unstable digit sort
options.explanation: Stability is still required for LSD passes; changing tie handling does not repair the signed-key encoding.

questions.workedExample: In two’s complement, the sign bit is one for negative integers and zero for nonnegative integers. XOR with a mask containing only the sign bit swaps those two encoding halves without rearranging the remaining bits. The resulting unsigned keys put negatives first, then nonnegatives. This is a fixed-width integer transform; floats require a different treatment and an explicit NaN policy.

lessons.title: Bucket sort and distribution assumptions
lessons.summary: Expected bucket performance depends on independent, roughly uniform keys.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Bucket sort

**Assumption:** keys are roughly **uniformly distributed** over a known range, for example floats in `[0, 1)`.

Create n buckets (one per element), each covering an equal slice of the range. Drop each element into its bucket, sort each bucket (with insertion sort), then concatenate. The bucket for a value is found by arithmetic, not comparison:

```formula
j = ⌊xn⌋
j = ⌊0.78 × 6⌋ = ⌊4.68⌋ = 4
where
j: the bucket number, from 0 to n − 1
x: the value being placed, at least 0 and less than 1; here 0.78
n: the number of elements, which is also the number of buckets; here 6
⌊ ⌋: the floor: round down to a whole number
In words: multiply the value by the number of buckets and round down; that picks the slice of [0, 1) the value falls in.
```

```python
def bucket_sort(a):  # floats in [0, 1)
    n = len(a)
    buckets = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for x in a:
        # Map the value to its equal-width
        # slice.
        buckets[int(x * n)].append(x)
    out = []
    for b in buckets:
        # Sort within a slice, then
        # concatenate.
        out.extend(sorted(b))
    return out
```

```
[0.78, 0.17, 0.39, 0.26, 0.72, 0.94]
6 buckets, width about 0.167
b0: []        b1: [0.17, 0.26]
b2: [0.39]    b3: []
b4: [0.78, 0.72]   b5: [0.94]
sort each, concat:
[0.17, 0.26, 0.39, 0.72, 0.78, 0.94]
```

With independent uniform input, each bucket has expected occupancy one, and the **expected** time is O(n). But it is only as good as the distribution assumption. If all values fall in one interval whose width is the reciprocal of the bucket count aligned with a bucket, one bucket receives all n values. Insertion sort there can cost O(n²); the shown Python version uses sorted(), so its worst-case bound is O(n log n). A fixed-width interval such as [0.50, 0.51) spans many buckets when n is large.

Bucket sort ideas show up in **histogram-based** and **sample sort** algorithms: sample the data to choose bucket boundaries that split it evenly. Distributed sorts (MapReduce's TeraSort, Spark's `sortBy`) do exactly this to divide data across machines.

## When to use which

| Situation | Choice |
|---|---|
| Small integer range (k not much above n) | Counting sort |
| Fixed-width ints, large n | LSD radix sort |
| Strings, variable length | MSD radix sort |
| Uniform real values | Bucket sort |
| Arbitrary comparator | Comparison sort |

In real systems:

- **NumPy:** `np.sort(kind='stable')` picks its algorithm by dtype. The NumPy 1.17 release notes, which introduced it, say radix sort is used for small integer types of **16 bits or less** and Timsort for the remaining types, including 32- and 64-bit integers. (The default `kind='quicksort'` is actually introsort.)
- **GPUs:** NVIDIA CUB offers radix sorting for supported keys; histogram, scan and scatter operations parallelize well. GPU libraries also support comparison-based sorting.
- **Databases:** some analytic engines radix-sort fixed-width encoded keys (such as normalised sort keys) instead of calling a comparator per pair.

## Pitfalls

1. **Memory.** Counting and LSD radix sorts need an O(n) output buffer plus O(k) or O(b) counters. They are not in place.
2. **Small n.** Passes and buffers can outweigh radix benefits for small inputs. **Content gap:** universal crossover sizes are omitted because they need measurements for a particular implementation, dtype and hardware.
3. **Wide or complex keys.** A composite key (last name, then first name, then date) or a locale-aware string collation requires an appropriate order-preserving encoding; ICU collation keys, for example, are byte sequences that can themselves be radix-sorted. Total key length and encoding cost matter. A comparison sort with a key function is simpler and often fast enough.
4. **Skewed data in bucket sort.** Real data is rarely uniform. Without sampling, buckets can be badly unbalanced.

## Key takeaways
- Expected bucket performance depends on independent, roughly uniform keys.
- Skew shifts work into the inner sort; library algorithms also depend on key type and implementation.

## Further reading
- [LSD and MSD radix sorting — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/51radix/)
- [NumPy sorting contracts](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.sort.html)
- [NumPy 1.17 historical dtype mapping](https://numpy.org/doc/1.17/release.html)

questions.prompt:
Which of these can realistically be sorted in **linear (or expected linear) time** with a non-comparison sort? Select all that apply.

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: 10 million `uint16` sensor readings
options.explanation: Correct. There are only 65,536 possible values, fewer than the 10 million readings, so counting sort (or one or two radix passes) is linear.

options.text: 1 million IPv4 addresses
options.explanation: Correct. They are 32-bit integers: LSD radix sort with 4 byte-sized passes.

options.text: 1 million names with locale-aware collation
options.explanation: No linear-in-record-count guarantee follows for arbitrary-length names. ICU can produce byte collation keys suitable for radix sorting, but key generation and total key length must be included.

options.text: 1 million floats drawn uniformly from [0, 1)
options.explanation: Correct. Bucket sort with n buckets runs in expected O(n) on uniform data (and radix sort on the float bit patterns also works).

options.text: 1 million objects ordered by an arbitrary user-supplied comparator
options.explanation: No. If all you have is a comparator, you're in the comparison model, and the Ω(n log n) lower bound applies (n is the number of objects).

questions.workedExample:
The question to ask is: **can I turn the key into small integer digits?**

- uint16: yes, directly (65,536 possible values).
- IPv4: yes, 4 bytes.
- Uniform floats: yes (or radix on bits); the bucket is computed, not compared:

```formula
j = ⌊xn⌋
where
j: the bucket index, 0 to n − 1
x: the float being placed, in [0, 1)
n: the number of buckets, one per value; here 1,000,000
⌊ ⌋: the floor: round down to a whole number
In words: multiply the value by the number of buckets and round down.
```

- Collated strings: byte collation keys are possible, but their lengths and generation costs are not bounded by the number of records.
- Arbitrary comparator: by definition, only comparisons are available.

questions.prompt:
Bucket sort (n buckets over [0, 1), insertion sort inside each bucket) is used on 100,000 latency values that have been scaled to [0, 1). Suppose 99% are independently uniform within [0.000, 0.001), presented in random order. At this fixed n, what cost increase should you expect?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: It still runs in O(n), since bucket sort is linear
options.explanation: Bucket sort is linear only in expectation under a uniform distribution. Skewed data breaks that assumption.

options.text: About 99,000 values land in the first ~100 buckets, so insertion sort inside them can do roughly 25 million shifts at this n
options.explanation: Correct. With 100,000 buckets of width 1/100,000 = 0.00001, [0, 0.001) spans 100 buckets holding ~990 values each. Insertion sort costs ~990²/4 per bucket, ≈ 25 million shifts total, versus ~100,000 for uniform data.

options.text: It fails with an error because buckets overflow
options.explanation: Buckets are dynamic lists; they grow. The problem is time, not errors.

options.text: It becomes O(n log n), the same as a comparison sort
options.explanation: With insertion sort inside buckets, crowded buckets cost quadratic time in their size, rather than logarithmic-factor linear time.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
w = 1 / n = 1 / 100000 = 0.00001
B = 0.001 / w = 100
m = 0.99n / B = 99000 / 100 = 990
S ≈ Bm^2 / 4 = 100 × 990^2 / 4
S ≈ 2.45 × 10^7
where
w: the width of one bucket
n: the number of values, and of buckets; here 100,000
B: the number of buckets the crowded range [0, 0.001) covers
m: the values per crowded bucket
S: the total insertion-sort shifts in the crowded buckets
m^2: m squared, m × m
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 99,000 values pile into 100 buckets of 990, and insertion sort's quadratic cost there adds up to about 24.5 million shifts.
```

1. Bucket width 0.00001, so the crowded range covers 100 buckets.
2. 99% of 100,000 = 99,000 values in those 100 buckets: about 990 per bucket.
3. Insertion sort on 990 random values: about 245,000 shifts each, ≈ 24.5 million in total.

Uniform data would have about 1 value per bucket, so around 100,000 operations. The estimated shift count is much larger; it does not establish a 250× wall-clock slowdown. With a fixed-width uniform subrange as n grows, expected time can still be O(n) with a larger constant. Fixes: choose bucket boundaries from a **sample** of the data (sample sort), use a log scale for latencies, or use a fallback sort inside large buckets.

questions.prompt:
Why do GPU sorting libraries such as NVIDIA's CUB typically use radix sort rather than quicksort or merge sort?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Its counting and scatter passes are data-parallel, so many GPU threads can process digits concurrently
options.explanation: Correct. Each pass is a histogram (count), a prefix sum (scan) and a scatter, all of which parallelise very well. GPU comparison sorts are also useful and can be efficient; supported key types and workload determine the choice.

options.text: Radix sort uses less memory than any comparison sort
options.explanation: LSD radix sort needs an O(n) output buffer (n is the number of keys), more than in-place quicksort. Memory isn't the reason.

options.text: GPUs cannot compare numbers
options.explanation: GPUs compare numbers perfectly well; branching on those comparisons is what is expensive when threads diverge.

options.text: Radix sort is stable, and GPUs require stability
options.explanation: LSD radix sort is stable, but that's a bonus, not the reason. GPUs have no stability requirement.

questions.workedExample:
One LSD pass breaks down into three bulk operations:

1. **Histogram:** every thread counts digit values for its chunk.
2. **Prefix sum (scan):** combine the counts into output offsets; there are well-known parallel scan algorithms.
3. **Scatter:** every element is written to its computed position.

None of these needs per-element branching on comparisons, so GPU threads stay in lockstep. With 32-bit keys and 8-bit digits, that's just 4 passes over the data.

lessons.title: Timsort runs and short-range insertion
lessons.summary: Run detection exploits existing order before merging.
lessons.body:
Textbook sorts assume random input. Real data is rarely random. Log files arrive nearly sorted by timestamp. A table is re-sorted after a few rows change. Two sorted lists are concatenated. A column has five distinct values across ten million rows.

Production sorts are **hybrid sorting algorithms** engineered to exploit that structure while keeping a worst-case guarantee. Throughout, n is the number of elements, and costs use Big O notation (O(n log n) grows like n times the base-2 logarithm of n, about 20 million for a million elements). This lesson covers the two most important designs, **Timsort** and **pdqsort**, what each mainstream language uses, and the bugs that come from comparators and stability rather than the algorithms.

## Timsort

Tim Peters wrote Timsort for Python in 2002. It became the object sort in Java 7, the sort in Android, V8 (Chrome and Node.js, since V8 7.0 in 2018) and Swift. It is a **stable, adaptive merge sort** built around **runs**.

### 1. Find natural runs

Scan for ascending or descending runs. In the original Timsort design, descending runs must be strictly decreasing before a plain reversal, because reversing equal elements breaks stability. CPython 3.14 also handles non-increasing runs by reversing equal-key subruns first, then reversing the whole run to restore tie order. The diagram below illustrates distinct keys.

```
[1, 4, 7, 9, 8, 5, 2, 3, 6]
 run A: 1 4 7 9 (ascending)
 run B: 8 5 2   (descending -> 2 5 8)
 run C: 3 6     (ascending)
```

### 2. Enforce a minimum run length

Merging lots of tiny runs is wasteful. CPython 3.14 computes a **minrun** between 32 and 64 for large arrays and extends short natural runs using **binary insertion sort**. For arrays shorter than 64 it detects the first run, then extends it to the whole array if needed. Other Timsort implementations use different thresholds.

On random data, most runs are extended to minrun; a final short remainder or a longer natural run can differ, and Timsort behaves like a well-tuned bottom-up merge sort.

## Key takeaways
- Run detection exploits existing order before merging.
- Reversing a descending run must preserve ties; short runs are extended with binary insertion sort.

## Further reading
- [Sorting techniques — Python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html)
- [CPython 3.14.0 list-sort design notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.14.0/Objects/listsort.txt)

questions.prompt:
Python's `list.sort()` is called on a list of 1,000,000 numbers that is **already sorted**. Approximately how many comparisons does Timsort make?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: About 1 million (n − 1)
options.explanation: Correct. Timsort's run detection scans the list once, finds a single ascending run covering everything, and has nothing to merge.

options.text: About 20 million (input size times its base-two logarithm)
options.explanation: That's plain merge sort's behaviour. Timsort detects natural runs, so sorted input needs no merging at all.

options.text: About 500 billion (half the squared input size)
options.explanation: Timsort has an O(n log n) worst case for n elements; it is never quadratic.

options.text: Zero, because Python caches that the list is sorted
options.explanation: Python lists don't track sortedness; Timsort has to look at every adjacent pair to discover the run.

questions.workedExample:
1. Timsort scans from the left for a run: it compares a[1] with a[0], a[2] with a[1], and so on.
2. On sorted input every comparison says "still ascending", so the run extends to the end: one comparison per adjacent pair, 999,999 in all.
3. One run on the stack: no merges.

Reverse-sorted input (with distinct elements) is equally cheap: one strictly descending run, reversed in place in time proportional to the number of elements.

questions.prompt:
Consider the original Timsort rule: reverse only **strictly** descending runs (`a[i] > a[i+1]`), with no separate handling of equal-key subruns. Why not also reverse runs like `[5, 4, 4, 3]`?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Strictly descending runs are faster to detect
options.explanation: Detection cost is the same either way; it's one comparison per step.

options.text: Reversing would swap the two equal 4s, breaking stability
options.explanation: Correct. Reversal flips the relative order of every pair, including equal ones, which a stable sort must not do. So the run stops at the first non-strict step.

options.text: Equal elements can't be part of any run
options.explanation: They can: ascending runs are non-decreasing (`a[i] <= a[i+1]`), so equal neighbours extend an ascending run.

options.text: Because reversing a run needs O(n) extra memory
options.explanation: Reversing a run of n elements in place uses O(1) memory, not O(n): swap from both ends towards the middle.

questions.workedExample:
Label the equal elements: `[5, 4a, 4b, 3]`.

If Timsort reversed it as a whole: `[3, 4b, 4a, 5]`. Now 4b precedes 4a, the opposite of the input. Unstable.

With the strict rule, the descending run is `[5, 4a]` (4a > 4b is false, so it stops). Reversed: `[4a, 5]`. Then `[4b, 3]` starts a new run, and the merge keeps 4a before 4b.

Ascending runs can include equal keys. Modern CPython also accepts non-increasing runs by first reversing equal-key subruns, then reversing the entire run, restoring tie order.

lessons.title: Timsort merge policies and galloping
lessons.summary: Merge only adjacent runs and use a policy that bounds pending work.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

### 3. Merge runs with a balanced policy

Runs are pushed onto a stack. Timsort merges only **adjacent** runs (merging non-adjacent ones would break stability) and chooses when to merge so that merges stay balanced and the stack stays small.

Classic Timsort uses run-length inequalities to keep pending runs growing geometrically toward the bottom of the stack:

```formula
|A| > |B| + |C|
|B| > |C|
where
A: the third run from the top of the run stack
B: the second run from the top
C: the run on top of the stack, the most recently found
|A|: the length of run A, in elements (likewise |B| and |C|)
>: greater than
In words: each pending run must be longer than the two above it combined, so lengths grow at least as fast as Fibonacci numbers and the stack stays short.
```

When an inequality fails, Timsort merges runs until both hold again. With runs of 15, 20 and 30 elements (C, B, A), the first rule fails because 30 is not greater than 20 + 15 = 35, so a merge happens. Correct collapse logic must maintain the intended invariant beyond just the top three runs. Stack capacity and policies differ by implementation; CPython uses powersort.

> [!warning] A proof found a bug
> In 2015, researchers formally verifying Java's `TimSort` with the KeY tool found that the merge-collapse rules did not always restore the invariant. On specially crafted arrays of around 67 million elements, the run stack overflowed with an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. Python fixed the rule; Java enlarged the stack. Since Python 3.11, CPython uses the **powersort** merge policy (Munro and Wild), which is provably near-optimal and simpler to reason about.

### 4. Gallop when one run is winning

During a normal merge, Timsort counts how many times in a row the output came from the same run. If that reaches `MIN_GALLOP` (initially 7), it switches to **galloping**: an exponential search checking positions 1, 3, 7, 15, ... then a binary search, to find how many elements it can copy in one block.

```formula
p_j = 2^j − 1
g ≈ 2 log_2(m)
g ≈ 2 log_2(500) ≈ 18
where
p_j: the position (offset from the start of the run) checked on probe number j: 1, 3, 7, 15, …
j: the probe number, 1, 2, 3, …
2^j: j copies of 2 multiplied together
g: the comparisons galloping needs to find where the other run's next element belongs
m: how many elements the winning run can copy in one block; 500 in the example below
log_2(m): the base-2 logarithm of m: how many doublings it takes to reach m (log_2(500) ≈ 9)
≈: approximately equal to
In words: about log_2(m) doubling probes overshoot the target, then about log_2(m) binary-search steps pin it down, instead of m one-by-one comparisons.
```

```
A: [1 2 3 4 5 ... 1000]
B: [500.5, 2000]
normal merge: ~500 comparisons for A's head
galloping: about 18 boundary comparisons
```

If galloping stops paying off, the threshold rises; if it keeps paying off, it falls. This adaptivity is why concatenating two sorted lists and sorting costs close to O(n), not O(n log n).

### Timsort's profile

In the table, n is the number of elements and k the number of natural runs in the input.

| Input | Cost |
|---|---|
| Already sorted / reversed | O(n): one run |
| k runs | O(n(1 + log k)) adaptive bound |
| Random | O(n log n), close to merge sort |
| Merge buffer | up to half the input elements; key caching and other metadata add storage |

Timsort minimises **comparisons**, which is exactly right for Python and JavaScript, where each comparison is a dynamic call that may run user code and costs far more than moving a pointer.

## Key takeaways
- Merge only adjacent runs and use a policy that bounds pending work.
- Galloping finds copy boundaries by exponential then binary search when one run keeps winning.

## Further reading
- [Sorting techniques — Python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html)
- [CPython 3.14.0 list-sort design notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.14.0/Objects/listsort.txt)
- [Formal verification of Java’s TimSort — de Gouw and colleagues](https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/23709/23709A.pdf)

lessons.title: pdqsort and language sorting contracts
lessons.summary: Pattern checks and bounded insertion attempts exploit favourable inputs.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## pdqsort

Orson Peters' **pattern-defeating quicksort** (2016, paper 2021) is the modern unstable sort. Go adopted it for `sort.Sort` in Go 1.19, and Rust used it for `sort_unstable` for years (Rust 1.81 replaced it with **ipnsort**, a successor by Peters and Bergdoll). It extends introsort with ideas that make common patterns fast:

- **Pivot selection**: median-of-three, or Tukey's ninther for larger arrays.
- **Partial insertion sort**: if partitioning detects an already partitioned range (excluding pivot setup), try insertion sort with a small cap on moves. On sorted or nearly sorted input this finishes in O(n).
- **Equal-element handling**: if the pivot equals the element just before the current sub-array, all elements equal to it are partitioned off in one pass. With k distinct keys the cost is O(nk), linear for few distinct values.
- **Bad-partition detection**: an unbalanced split triggers a shuffle of a few elements to break adversarial patterns. After a logarithmic budget of bad partitions, it falls back to heapsort, guaranteeing O(n log n).
- **Branchless block partitioning** (from BlockQuicksort) for cheap comparisons such as integers, avoiding branch mispredictions on random data.

The result: O(n log n) worst case, in place, and linear on sorted, reversed and all-equal inputs.

## What your language actually uses

| Language | Default | Stable? |
|---|---|---|
| Python `sorted`, `list.sort` | Timsort (powersort merges) | Yes |
| Java objects, `List.sort` | TimSort | Yes |
| Java primitives | Dual-pivot quicksort | n/a |
| JavaScript `Array.sort` | Timsort in V8 | Yes |
| C++ `std::sort` | Typically introsort-family; implementation-specific | No |
| C++ `std::stable_sort` | Typically merge-based; implementation-specific | Yes |
| Rust `sort` / `sort_unstable` | driftsort / ipnsort | Yes / No |
| Go `sort.Sort`, `slices.Sort` | pdqsort | No |

Notes on the table:

- Java sorts primitives with an unstable quicksort because equal `int`s are indistinguishable, so stability is invisible. Objects need stability, so they get TimSort.
- JavaScript only **required** a stable sort from ES2019; older engines differed.
- Go provides `sort.Stable` and `slices.SortStableFunc` when you need stability.
- C's `qsort` specifies neither the algorithm nor stability.

## Key takeaways
- Pattern checks and bounded insertion attempts exploit favourable inputs.
- Know whether stability and complexity are API guarantees or implementation choices.

## Further reading
- [pdqsort design and guarantees — project documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/orlp/pdqsort/master/readme.md)
- [Go 1.19 sorting implementation change](https://go.dev/doc/go1.19)
- [Slice sorting contracts — Rust documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.slice.html)
